summary.text: Black-body radiation is the heat glow given off by a body in thermal balance with its surroundings, and a black body is an idealized object that absorbs all light that hits it.
Its spectrum is continuous and depends only on temperature, peaking at higher frequencies as the body gets hotter.
That is why a heated object glows dull red, then orange, yellow and finally bluish-white, and why the Sun can be roughly treated as a black body.

facts.label: Name coined
facts.value: Gustav Kirchhoff introduced the term black body in 1860

facts.label: Dull red glow
facts.value: Around 500 degrees Celsius, objects begin to glow visibly

facts.label: The Sun
facts.value: Effective temperature of about 5800 K, peaked in yellow-green light

facts.label: Lab approximation
facts.value: A small hole in a hot closed box gives near-ideal radiation

facts.label: No perfect case
facts.value: Perfect black bodies do not exist in nature

items.prompt: A blacksmith heats a steel bar. At first it is invisible in the light, then glows dull red, later yellow. What mainly changes between these stages?

options.label: The bar's temperature, which shifts its emitted light to higher frequencies
The bar's mass, which changes the color it reflects
The room's brightness, which tints the metal
The hammer's force, which makes the metal release colors

items.explain: The spectrum peaks at a frequency that shifts higher as temperature rises, so the glow goes from red toward yellow and white.

items.prompt: Two oven walls are built from different materials, but both are well sealed and held at the same temperature. What can you say about the light from a small opening?

options.label: The material with darker color gives a different color
Heavier walls produce a redder spectrum
The color depends on the cavity temperature alone
Metal walls produce a brighter spectrum than ceramic ones

items.explain: As long as almost all light entering is absorbed, the spectrum and color come out as a function of cavity temperature alone.

items.prompt: A person in a dark room with a normal-looking object at room temperature, like a cup. Where does most of its thermal radiation fall?

options.label: In visible red light that the eye can easily see
In ultraviolet light that can tan skin
Exactly in the green part of the visible band
In the infrared, which people cannot see

items.explain: At room temperature a black body radiates mostly in the infrared, which the human eye cannot perceive.

items.prompt: A metal piece in a furnace looks white-hot. What does that tell you about its emission?

options.label: A substantial share of its energy is going out as ultraviolet
It is cooler than when it was glowing red
It has stopped emitting infrared light entirely
It must be reflecting the furnace walls only

items.explain: When a body appears white it is emitting a substantial fraction of its energy as ultraviolet radiation, and it is hotter than a red-glowing one.

items.prompt: Why is a closed graphite box with a tiny hole a good stand-in for an ideal black body?

options.label: Graphite makes new light matching ideal spectra
Light entering the hole is nearly all absorbed inside
The hole lets heat leak out so the box stays cold
Graphite reflects every color equally back out

items.explain: Any cavity built so that almost all light entering is absorbed by its walls holds a good approximation to black-body radiation.

items.prompt: The Sun and Earth are not in perfect thermal balance with their surroundings. Is black-body radiation still useful for them?

options.label: No, because the idea only works for objects in perfect balance
No, because stars give off no thermal radiation
Yes, but only for objects at room temperature
Yes, as a good first approximation of their energy output

items.explain: Even though planets and stars are neither in equilibrium nor perfect black bodies, black-body radiation is a good first approximation for their emitted energy.
